candidates.title: Improvement to parts-status gates: retain ownership until updates are completed
candidates.proposal:
Preserve the parts-status gate process, but close a consequential execution gap: recording a next-update commitment does not ensure either staff member delivers it when work is interrupted or handed over. The mechanism remains evidence-gated estimating; the improvement makes its customer commitments executable.

Review the 30 records and supplier replies for usable delivery and repair timings. On each paper card record the latest parts evidence and timestamp, any supported pickup window, its conditions, the next customer-update deadline and one named owner. Before parts receipt, give a conditional window only where supplier evidence and repair capacity support it; otherwise give status and an update commitment. Confirm timing after the correct parts are received, checked and scheduled.

One staff member checks the inbox twice daily. Keep cards needing updates together, with the earliest deadline first. Ownership transfers only when the other staff member initials acceptance; until then, the original owner remains responsible. An interrupted call stays visibly unfinished. At each inbox review, check unfinished updates before making new commitments.

If supplier information is missing when an update is due, the owner still contacts the customer with the known status and uncertainty. If evidence invalidates a pickup window, disclose that promptly. Record unsuccessful contact attempts and retry at the next review; neither an attempt nor an unanswered message establishes customer understanding. On the customer's next incoming contact, resolve the outstanding update first.

This requires paper fields, the existing inbox and brief coordination. It assumes customers have provided a usable contact route. It cannot resolve supplier uncertainty or guarantee contact. If the owner is unavailable, the other staff member takes ownership explicitly during the next review; urgent threatened commitments take priority over routine administration.
candidates.experiment:
For four weeks, alternate eligible new jobs between this version and ordinary evidence gates with recorded update deadlines. Both disclose delays honestly. One staff member owns the comparison log. Tally misses against original pickup windows, inbound status calls and all staff minutes, including failed contact attempts and handoff administration. Also record estimate availability, lead time, overdue updates and unresolved jobs.

Inspect the first five interrupted or transferred updates: did responsibility remain identifiable and did the customer receive an update? Stop the added handoff procedure if it consumes time without reducing overdue updates, or repeatedly displaces urgent repair work; retain evidence gates and direct ownership. Four weeks may establish feasibility rather than a reliable effect on missed estimates.

candidates.title: Prepare authorized repair work while parts are in transit
candidates.proposal:
Reduce the uncertain work remaining after delivery by completing useful, independent repair tasks during the parts wait. The primary mechanism is changing the repair sequence: expose additional faults and finish permissible preparation earlier, so parts arrival leaves a smaller, better-understood path to pickup.

Use the 30 job records and supplier replies to look for repairs where work after receipt took longer because inspection or independent preparation had been deferred. Missing task timings cannot establish that this problem exists. Begin only with a recurring repair type where the staff can identify a safe, worthwhile task that does not require the replacement part.

During the existing diagnosis and customer authorization conversation, the diagnosing staff member identifies which tasks are already covered by the agreed repair. On the paper card, separate work that can safely proceed now from work requiring the part and final testing. Examples might include an accessible inspection or cleaning already included in the repair. Do not add chargeable scope, leave equipment unsafe or dismantled indefinitely, or start work whose compatibility depends on an unverified part.

Use otherwise uncommitted workshop time for that preparation. The person doing it records completion and findings; the other staff member checks the card before communicating timing. New faults trigger an explanation and any necessary authorization before extra work. Pickup windows still require current supplier evidence, realistic remaining labor and workshop capacity. Unknown delivery means pickup remains unconfirmed, with a recorded next-update commitment.

If no safe independent task exists, continue the ordinary evidence-gated process. If preparation is interrupted, record the equipment's condition and next safe action before switching jobs. After receipt, verify the part, complete dependent work and testing, then confirm collection. This needs existing repair tools, paper and the inbox. Its value depends on spare capacity and genuinely reusable preparation; cancellations, storage and repeated setup could erase the benefit.
candidates.experiment:
One staff member owns a four-week trial, alternating eligible jobs between early preparation and the ordinary sequence, with identical evidence requirements and delay disclosure. Compare missed original pickup windows, inbound status calls and total staff minutes. Also record estimate availability and lead time, receipt-to-ready time, repeated setup, wasted preparation and displacement of already promised work.

Inspect the first five prepared jobs: did completed work remain useful and reduce the work remaining after receipt? Stop early preparation if it threatens an existing supported commitment, creates unsafe storage, or repeatedly adds labor without shortening completion time or improving estimates. Continue collecting outcomes for all enrolled jobs, marking unfinished jobs separately. A lack of eligible tasks or spare capacity is evidence against using this process routinely.
